analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to protect workers from dangerous heat with water, shade, paid breaks, and training.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2023 with 25 Senate cosponsors, referred to the HELP Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the Labor Department to write a national rule making employers protect workers from heat. Employers would have had to provide cool drinking water, access to shade or cool-down areas, paid rest breaks, and training in the language workers understand, and would have faced stronger penalties for violations. It never got a committee hearing or vote in the Senate and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Outdoor and hot-industry workers—farmworkers, construction crews, warehouse and delivery workers, landscaping and sanitation crews—would gain enforceable protections: water, shade, paid rest breaks, acclimatization schedules, language-accessible training, and whistleblower protections. Workers already covered by state heat rules (like California's) would gain a federal floor that no state could undercut.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Outdoor and hot-warehouse workers, especially farmworkers

how_it_helps.text: It directs the Secretary of Labor to issue a binding national heat protection standard within one year, requiring employers to provide cool drinking water, paid rest breaks, access to shade or cool-down areas, and acclimatization policies where engineering fixes cannot reduce heat to safe levels [S2].
It requires that any mandated rest breaks, training, or medical removal be paid at the worker's regular rate, so protection does not come out of workers' paychecks [S2].

It requires training and heat plans in a language workers understand, and updates the National Agricultural Workers Survey to track heat illness—provisions aimed at farmworkers, who face some of the highest heat risks [S2].
It adds whistleblower protections so workers who report heat hazards cannot legally be fired or retaliated against, and allows a 4-year window for issuing citations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers in agriculture, construction, warehousing, delivery, and other heat-exposed industries would bear the cost of water, shade or cooling space, paid breaks, training, and written heat illness prevention plans, plus enforcement exposure under a four-year citation window.
analysis.who_pays_short: Agriculture, construction, and other heat-exposed employers

drawbacks.text: The bill orders the Labor Department to issue an interim final rule within one year without normal notice-and-comment review and without regard to the Paperwork Reduction Act, which critics would say leaves too little time for employers to weigh in on rules that could require costly changes like cooling equipment or schedule changes.

Compliance costs fall on employers, including small farms and contractors, for water, shade, cooling equipment, paid rest breaks, training, and written heat plans; the bill also extends the statute of limitations for citations to four years and directs courts and the review commission to defer to the Secretary's interpretations, tilting enforcement disputes toward the government [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete: a federal heat standard would require the cheapest, most proven protections—water, shade, paid breaks, acclimatization—at modest employer cost, and heat deaths are preventable with well-understood measures. The costs are real but limited: compliance burdens fall on employers, especially small farms and construction firms, and the bill's fast one-year interim rule (bypassing normal review procedures) plus a four-year enforcement window and shifted legal deference are aggressive designs that courts and business groups would contest. On balance, the health gains for millions of exposed workers outweigh those costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate HELP Committee in July 2023 and sat there, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote, until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sherrod Brown introduced the bill in the Senate on July 26, 2023; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, the only action it ever received [S1][S4].
No further action appears in the record through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025: no hearing, no committee vote, no Senate floor vote [S4].

The bill would have required the Labor Department to issue an enforceable heat standard covering water, shade, paid rest breaks, training, and whistleblower protections within a year of enactment [S2].
The bill is named for Asunción Valdivia, a farmworker who died after working in extreme heat, though the provided sources do not detail his case.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in agriculture, construction, warehousing, and delivery who would have borne the cost of a mandatory federal heat standard are better off because the bill died, while workers in hot jobs continue without federal heat protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers facing no federal heat standard

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 25 cosponsors, all Democrats plus one independent.

for.name: Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor named in the introduction, alongside 17 other senators [S1][S3].

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.role: Senate majority opponents of expanded OSHA rulemaking
against.what_they_did: Republicans controlled the legislative agenda's chokepoints through their HELP Committee members and filibuster posture; the bill received no hearing or markup. No individual senator is on record in the provided sources as blocking it.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, so the bill never had a plausible path to the 60 votes needed to overcome a Senate filibuster.

industries.note: Farm operations would face binding federal requirements for water, shade, paid breaks, training, and heat plans for field workers. These costs are small relative to payroll but fall on some of the lowest-margin employers.
Construction and other outdoor employers would bear compliance costs for heat protections and training. The burden is real but applies only where heat exposure is hazardous.
The bill would tighten standards for temporary labor camps and require language-access protections for temp workers, a group often excluded from employer obligations.
